```{r setup, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 7,
                      fig.height = 4.6, out.width = "100%", dpi = 110)
options(digits = 4)
```

Attribution packages consume journeys: `"display > social > paid_search"`
strings with conversion counts attached. Producing those strings from a raw
event log is usually left to the analyst: `ChannelAttribution`, for instance,
starts from the aggregated paths, on the reasonable grounds that its job is
Markov removal effects and it does that in C++.

So the step gets done in analysis code, usually as a `group_by()` and a
`paste(collapse = " > ")`. This vignette is about what that loses, which is
not small, and then about dividing credit among channels once the journeys
are right.

```{r}
library(mediamix)
data(mm_events)

nrow(mm_events)
head(mm_events)
```

`mm_events` is a synthetic log of
`r format(nrow(mm_events), big.mark = ",")` touchpoint events across
`r format(length(unique(mm_events$customer_id)), big.mark = ",")` customers.
It contains, on purpose, everything a real export contains: repeat
converters, consecutive duplicate channels, direct and blank and missing
channel labels, customers who never convert, timestamp ties, and rows in no
particular order.

## The naive approach

One path per customer, in timestamp order:

```{r}
ordered <- mm_events[order(mm_events$customer_id, mm_events$timestamp), ]
naive <- split(ordered$channel, ordered$customer_id)

c(journeys = length(naive), mean_length = mean(lengths(naive)))
```

`r format(length(naive), big.mark = ",")` journeys at a mean length of
`r round(mean(lengths(naive)), 2)`. Now the same log through `build_paths()`,
with its default settings:

```{r}
paths <- build_paths(
  mm_events,
  id = "customer_id",
  channel = "channel",
  timestamp = "timestamp",
  conversion = "conversion",
  value = "value"
)
summary_built <- path_summary(paths)
summary_built
```

`r format(summary_built$journeys, big.mark = ",")` journeys,
`r round(100 * (summary_built$journeys / length(naive) - 1))`% more, at a mean
length of `r round(summary_built$mean_length, 2)`,
`r round(100 * (1 - summary_built$mean_length / mean(lengths(naive))))`%
shorter. Journey counts and lengths feed a Markov transition matrix directly,
so differences of this size carry through to the final numbers.

Here is where the difference comes from, one concern at a time.

```{r}
step <- function(...) {
  s <- path_summary(build_paths(
    mm_events, id = "customer_id", channel = "channel",
    timestamp = "timestamp", conversion = "conversion", ...))
  c(journeys = s$journeys, mean_length = round(s$mean_length, 2))
}

steps <- rbind(
  `naive`                       = c(length(naive), round(mean(lengths(naive)), 2)),
  `split on conversion`         = step(split_on = "conversion",
                                       collapse_repeats = FALSE),
  `+ 30-day inactivity gap`     = step(split_on = c("conversion", "gap"),
                                       gap = 30, collapse_repeats = FALSE),
  `+ collapse duplicates`       = step(split_on = c("conversion", "gap"),
                                       gap = 30, collapse_repeats = TRUE)
)
steps
```

Splitting on conversion accounts for every extra journey. The three
`build_paths()` rows also drop the `r summary_built$duplicate_events` exact
duplicate events in the log (`dedupe = TRUE`, the default). The 30-day
inactivity split changes nothing here: every gap that long in this log comes
straight after a conversion, where the journey has already been split.
Collapsing consecutive duplicates shortens the journeys further.

## The seven things that go wrong

### 1. Journey splitting

A customer who converts in March and again in September is two journeys. Treat
them as one and March's touchpoints take credit for September's sale, while
the journey count falls by every repeat conversion in the file.

```{r}
repeat_buyers <- table(mm_events$customer_id[mm_events$conversion == 1])
table(as.integer(repeat_buyers))
```

The table counts converting customers by how many times they converted. Here
`r sum(repeat_buyers > 1)` converted more than once, for
`r sum(repeat_buyers - 1)` repeat conversions, and the naive approach finds
`r summary_built$journeys - length(naive)` fewer journeys than `build_paths()`.

`build_paths()` splits on conversion by default (`split_on = "conversion"`).
`split_on` also accepts `"gap"`, so a customer who disappears for four months
and comes back starts a new journey rather than extending an eleven-month one.

### 2. Lookback windows

A touch two years before a conversion did not cause it. Thirty, sixty and
ninety days are the standard choices, and none of them came from your data.

`conversion_lag()` measures how long converting journeys take, from first
touch to conversion, so you can read the window off your own data instead:

```{r}
lags <- conversion_lag(paths)
lags
```

Ninety per cent of converting journeys in this log complete within about
`r round(lags$lag[lags$quantile == 0.9])` days, so a 30-day window truncates
almost nothing and a 90-day window is pure decoration. The tail is real,
though: the slowest journey takes `r round(max(lags$lag))` days, so a window is
a decision about which tail to discard, not a free simplification. On a
considered-purchase category the same table may tell you the opposite, and
reading it takes one line.

### 3. Non-converting journeys

These null paths are kept by default (`keep_null_paths = TRUE`), and you
should think hard before changing that. `as_channel_paths()` counts them for
each distinct path, beside its conversions:

```{r}
with_nulls <- as_channel_paths(paths)
head(with_nulls, 4)
c(converting = sum(with_nulls$total_conversions),
  null = sum(with_nulls$total_null))
```

`r format(sum(with_nulls$total_null), big.mark = ",")` of the
`r format(summary_built$journeys, big.mark = ",")` journeys here never
converted. Markov removal effects, covered below, are computed *against* the
null paths: the transition matrix needs an absorbing failure state to compare
the conversion state with. Drop them and the conversion probability becomes 1,
so every removal effect is measured against the wrong baseline and moves up or
down depending on how the dropped journeys differ from the converting ones.
`markov_removal()` warns when a table has none.

### 4. Direct, none and missing channels

Every real log has them, and every tutorial handles them differently. Here
`direct = "label"` folds them into one channel:

```{r}
table(build_paths(mm_events, id = "customer_id", channel = "channel",
                  timestamp = "timestamp", conversion = "conversion",
                  direct = "label")$channel)
```

`"keep"`, the default, leaves the labels alone (naming the unnamed ones
`"(blank)"` and `"(missing)"` so they can be referred to at all), `"label"`
folds them into the one `"(direct)"` channel above, and `"drop"` removes those
touches entirely. The choice moves the numbers, so it is an argument rather
than fixed behaviour buried in the source.

### 5. Accounting for what gets dropped

Dropping direct traffic can strip a converting journey of every touchpoint it
had, including, sometimes, the touch that recorded the conversion. mediamix
fixes the conversion facts before any filtering, so the conversion is never
erased; it is counted and reported as unattributable. A short lookback makes
this more common, because the window is measured back from the conversion even
when the converting touch itself is dropped. Here direct traffic is dropped
and the lookback cut to one day:

```{r}
dropped <- build_paths(
  mm_events, id = "customer_id", channel = "channel",
  timestamp = "timestamp", conversion = "conversion",
  lookback = 1, direct = "drop"
)
path_summary(dropped)[, c("conversions_observed", "converting_journeys",
                          "conversions_unattributable")]
```

Those `r path_summary(dropped)$conversions_unattributable` conversions
happened. They cannot be credited to any channel under these settings, and a
pipeline that quietly reports a smaller denominator is lying by omission.

### 6. Consecutive duplicates

Three page views on the same channel are usually one exposure recorded three
times. Collapsing them is what takes the mean journey length from
`r steps["+ 30-day inactivity gap", "mean_length"]` to
`r steps["+ collapse duplicates", "mean_length"]` in the table above.
`collapse_repeats = TRUE`, the default, keeps the *first* touch of each run,
preserving when the channel entered the journey. If you are using
`credit_time_decay()`, consider `FALSE`, since keeping the first of a run
pushes each channel's apparent recency backward.

### 7. Deterministic ordering

Logs written at second resolution are full of ties. `build_paths()` breaks
them by original row order, except that a conversion sorts after every touch
sharing its timestamp, so the same input always gives the same journeys.
Without a fixed tie-break, first-touch and last-touch results are not
reproducible.

## Assigning credit

mediamix has five credit rules: `credit_first()`, `credit_last()`,
`credit_linear()`, `credit_position()` and `credit_time_decay()`, plus
`credit_custom()` for your own. Each returns the journey table with a `credit`
column, so they can be compared side by side.

```{r}
lin <- credit_linear(paths)
head(lin[, c("path_id", "channel", "touch_rank", "touch_n", "credit")])
```

Credit sums to 1 within every converting journey, and total credit equals the
number of attributable conversions. That invariant catches journeys silently
dropped in construction:

```{r}
c(total_credit = sum(lin$credit),
  attributable = path_summary(paths)$converting_journeys)
```

`attribute()` runs the five rules and the Markov model described below at
once, which is the point:

```{r}
res <- attribute(paths)
head(res, 8)
```

Each row is one rule and channel: `conversions` is the credit the channel
received, `share` its fraction of that rule's total, `value` the conversion
value credited to it, and `touches` the channel's touchpoints in every
journey, converting or not.

## The spread is the finding

Any single rule gives you a number. Several rules give you the range that
number could have been, which is more honest and usually more useful:

```{r}
spread <- attribution_spread(res)
spread
```

`plot()` draws the same table for the six channels with the largest mean
share. Each bar is the range a channel's share covers across all six rules,
with the first-touch, last-touch and Markov shares marked:

```{r spread-plot}
plot(res, n = 6)
```

Display's share runs from
`r round(100 * spread$min_share[spread$channel == "display"])`% under
last-touch to `r round(100 * spread$max_share[spread$channel == "display"])`%
under first-touch, depending only on the convention chosen. That channel has
not been measured; it has been assigned a number. Paid search and email move
the other way, with their largest shares under last-touch.
`channel_positions()` says why. It counts how often each channel is the only,
first, middle or last touch of a converting journey:

```{r}
positions <- channel_positions(paths)
positions
```

Display opens journeys: it appears first about
`r round(positions$first_last_ratio[positions$channel == "display"])` times for
every time it appears last, while paid search and email close them. First-touch
and last-touch attribution therefore disagree about them by construction, and
reporting either one alone is choosing a side of that disagreement without
saying so.

Both tables carry a column called `first_last_ratio`, and they are different
quantities. Here it is a ratio of touchpoint *counts*
(`r round(positions$first_last_ratio[positions$channel == "display"], 2)` for
display); in `attribution_spread()` above it is a ratio of credited *shares*
(`r round(spread$first_last_ratio[spread$channel == "display"], 2)`). Both say
display opens journeys; they are measured in different currencies and will
not agree numerically.

The assist matrix from `assisted_conversions()` is the other half of the
picture:

```{r}
real <- c("display", "social", "organic_search", "paid_search", "email")
assists <- assisted_conversions(paths, normalise = TRUE)
round(assists[real, real], 3)
```

Read a row as "this channel assisted these channels". Display precedes paid
search in `r round(100 * assists["display", "paid_search"])`% of the converting
journeys display appears in; paid search precedes display in only
`r round(100 * assists["paid_search", "display"])`% of its own. That asymmetry
is the same finding as the first-versus-last ratio, seen pairwise rather than
in aggregate.

## Time decay, and the connection to adstock

`credit_time_decay()` spreads a conversion's credit backward across prior
touchpoints with geometric decay, the same kernel `adstock_geometric()` uses
to spread spend forward, and the same `decay` vocabulary. Here the half-life
is three days:

```{r}
td <- credit_time_decay(paths, decay = decay_from_half_life(3))
example <- td[td$path_id == td$path_id[td$converted & td$touch_n >= 4][1], ]
example[, c("channel", "touch_rank", "time_to_conversion", "credit")]
```

A touch's credit halves for every three days between it and the conversion.
That symmetry with adstock is not a coincidence: `vignette("spine")` puts the
two kernels side by side and shows where the symmetry stops.

## Data-driven attribution: Markov removal effects

The five rules above are conventions chosen in advance. The Markov model of
Anderl et al. (2016) lets the journeys choose instead. It fits a transition
matrix from start, through channels, to conversion or null, and credits each
channel by its *removal effect*: the proportional fall in the probability of
converting when every transition into that channel is sent to null instead.

`markov_removal()` fits the order-1 model exactly, from the absorbing-chain
fundamental matrix, in base R:

```{r}
mk <- markov_removal(paths)
mk
attr(mk, "p_conversion")
```

`p_conversion` is the baseline, the model's probability that a journey
converts, and each channel's `conversions` are the converting journeys divided
in proportion to the removal effects. The null paths are what make this work:
they are how the model learns how often a journey ends in nothing, which is
why `build_paths()` keeps them by default. `attribute()` runs this model as
its `"markov"` rule, so the spread table above already included it:

```{r}
res[res$rule == "markov", c("channel", "conversions", "share")]
```

Markov attribution is still not incrementality. Removing a state from a chain
assumes every customer who would have passed through it is lost and none finds
another route to the same purchase. It is a more data-driven convention than
first-touch, and a convention nonetheless.

## Handing off to ChannelAttribution

For higher-order chains, `ChannelAttribution` estimates the same removal
effects in C++. `as_channel_paths()` exports the journeys in exactly the
format it expects:

```{r}
# ChannelAttribution splits paths on ">", so export with the same separator.
ca <- as_channel_paths(paths, sep = ">")
head(ca, 4)
```

```{r ca, eval = requireNamespace("ChannelAttribution", quietly = TRUE)}
ChannelAttribution::markov_model(
  ca, var_path = "path",
  var_conv = "total_conversions", var_null = "total_null", sep = ">"
)
```

```{r eval = !requireNamespace("ChannelAttribution", quietly = TRUE), echo = FALSE, comment = NA}
cat("ChannelAttribution is not installed, so the chunk above was not run.\n")
```

For `order = 1`, ChannelAttribution and `markov_removal()` should agree up to
ChannelAttribution's simulation error.

## What attribution cannot tell you

Rule-based attribution is a bookkeeping convention, not a causal estimate. It
divides observed conversions among observed touchpoints according to a rule you
chose. It cannot tell you what would have happened if a channel had not run,
because that outcome is not in the log. No rule, however sophisticated,
recovers a counterfactual from data that does not contain one. Only an
experiment, or a credible quasi-experiment, does.

Well-built journeys make the bookkeeping honest, comparable across rules, and
reproducible. That is worth a great deal. It is not incrementality.

## References

Anderl, E., Becker, I., von Wangenheim, F. and Schumann, J. H. (2016). Mapping
the customer journey: Lessons learned from graph-based online attribution
modeling. *International Journal of Research in Marketing*, 33(3), 457–474.
